leads.name: The Westersingel Plane

location.address: Westersingel, moved from the west to the east side of the canal in the 1960s

leads.story: Moving a mature tree across a street sounds like a euphemism for felling it and planting a new one, but Rotterdam actually did it: sometime in the 1960s, engineers transplanted this plane tree bodily from the west side of the Westersingel canal to the east side, roots and all, rather than lose it to whatever roadworks or redesign prompted the move. It survived the operation and kept growing, now roughly 130 years old and widely considered one of Rotterdam's most impressive individual trees, a status confirmed in 2021 when it placed second in the Netherlands' national Tree of the Year competition, a public vote that draws entries from across the country. The achievement is not really about beauty or age alone. Rotterdam has fewer monumental trees than almost any comparable Dutch city, a direct consequence of the 1940 bombing that flattened its historic centre and the soft, subsiding soil across much of the region that shortens most trees' working lives regardless of what happens above ground. A plane tree that not only reached this size but survived being dug up and relocated says something about the species' famous toughness along waterways, and about a city that has had unusually good reason to fight for the few old trees it has left.
leads.access: Free, public street at any time
leads.transport: Walkable from central Rotterdam, roughly 10 minutes
leads.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the one that was dug up and moved: it grew on the west side of the Westersingel until the 1960s. It stands on the east bank now, and came second in the 2021 national Tree of the Year vote.

blocked.name: Gewone plataan Park Euromast
blocked.reason: Probable duplicate of already-published rot_001 (The Park Plane), not delivered as new. LRMB register nr 1690283 sits about 185m from rot_001's published coordinates, described as 'A/d vijver bij voorm. disco' (by the pond near the former disco) versus rot_001's sourced location 'on the grass field near the Westzeedijk'; different named spots within the same 21-hectare Het Park, which on its own would argue for two distinct trees. But the register's own history text for this entry recites the same unusual narrative beats as rot_001's source (hetparkinrotterdam.nl): the two 1850s estates merged into the park, Zocher's design, trees too thick to fell for firewood in WWII, and specifically 'Deze plataan overleefde de overstroming' (survived the 1953 flood) -- the exact same flood-survival detail used for rot_001's tree. Rotterdam's own official monumental-trees highlight page (rotterdam.nl/monumentale-bomen) lists only ONE plane tree for 'Park bij de Euromast' ('one of the thickest trees in the city', matching rot_001), not two. Two attempts to reach monumentaltrees.com's page for this park (which might disambiguate) both returned 403 (site blocks automated fetches, as documented). Given the shared narrative and the absence of a second named plane in either the municipal highlight page or any other source found, treated as the same tree with an imprecise register coordinate rather than a genuinely separate specimen. If a future pass or a reader on the ground confirms Het Park holds two distinct old monumental planes (one at the Westzeedijk grass field, one by the pond near the former disco site), this should be revisited and delivered as a new tree.

blocked.name: Ginkgo Heemraadssingel Rotterdam
blocked.reason: Private land, hard rule 10. LRMB register nr 1697008 places this tree in the 'achtertuin' (back garden) of a private residential building at Heemraadssingel 289 (owner_category particulier). No independent source found confirming the tree is visible or accessible from the street/canal path, despite two search attempts; the register's own 'visible: ja' likely reflects the register surveyor's own visit rather than public visibility. Register history notes it may be Rotterdam's oldest Ginkgo biloba (planted shortly after the house was built in 1912, survived a 1940 bomb that fell in the garden) -- a good story, but not one we can send visitors to without confirmed public access. Also only one source (the register) was found, short of the two-source bar. Leave as a lead: if a reader or a future pass confirms it is visible over the garden wall from the singel, or the address is now a business/institution rather than a private home, revisit.
